title: Back to the Last Drop
summary: The trio deliberately backtracks to the Last Drop to see what became of Varnok after they left. Eva expects to test Veyra's manipulation; Jessa expects a town to have done whatever towns do with a good story.

panelPlan.text: The Last Drop appears from the road, visually familiar but socially altered: more people outside, Marcus's old enforcers no longer owning the porch.
Eva rehearses competing theories from the rear seat while Jessa drives. Kael asks whether either theory changes where they are parking.
They stop short when they see a rough painted figure on the saloon wall: a black-coated Varnok cutting a rope.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: My guess: Samuel stopped at every watering hole between here and Cinder Basin.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessa
dialogueInline.text: My guess: people don't need Samuel to gossip.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You don't even know what it is.

directionInline.text: Backtracking should feel like returning to living people, not revisiting a clue location. The altered social atmosphere is the first answer.

title: Varnok Stayed
summary: The man Kael cut down is recovering and now openly works around the Last Drop. He tells them Marcus lost control after the hanging, but the town credits 'Varnok' for the change even though Tomas knows Kael gave a different name.

panelPlan.text: Tomas carries a tray awkwardly, rope scars still visible. He recognizes Kael immediately and calls him Kael, startling Eva more than another false name would.
Inside, patrons toast Varnok as a man who came back, broke Marcus's hold and vanished again. The story has become communal property.
Kael asks Tomas whether Marcus is dead. Tomas says no; he simply left when people stopped being afraid of him.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: Marcus left three days after you did.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: People say Varnok ran him off.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: People like a face on a story.

directionInline.text: Tomas anchors reality. He knows Kael is Kael and still understands why the town prefers the Varnok story.

title: One Seed, Twenty Stories
summary: Samuel confirms exactly what he planted at the Last Drop: the Varnok name, a rough description of Kael and the day he expected Kael to pass through. Everything after Kael arrived, including the heroic biography and political afterlife of Varnok, developed without Samuel.

panelPlan.text: At a back table, Tomas sketches the chain of gossip: scarred patron to bartender, bartender to two families, two families to the workers Marcus had threatened.
Samuel confirms the seed Eva found on the first trip: name, rough description and expected day. Veyra then asks who added later details and quickly runs out of clean answers.
Eva is delighted by the branching story until Jessa points out that none of the branches belong to Kael anymore.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I gave Harker the name. Dark coat. Black hair. The day I thought Kael would come through.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: By supper, Varnok had a dead brother.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: Woman who improves any story she hears.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: You lit a match. Town supplied the furniture.

directionInline.text: Keep the causal boundary exact. Samuel created the initial appointment at the Last Drop; the town created the Varnok mythology that followed. This must remain consistent with Eva's dated scrap from Issue 1.

title: The Man on the Wall
summary: Kael confronts the crude mural of Varnok modeled on what people remember about him. Eva initially treats it as fascinating evidence; Kael sees a version of himself the town can use without him.

panelPlan.text: Outside, the mural exaggerates Kael into a broad-shouldered avenger with a red sun behind him. It is obviously folk art, not a magical likeness.
Eva compares details to Kael while Jessa watches his expression and realizes he genuinely dislikes it.
Tomas explains that the image helps people remember the day Marcus stopped owning the porch. Kael accepts the need without accepting the identity.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: It isn't meant to be you exactly.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: It's the day Marcus lost the porch.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kael
dialogueInline.text: They remember what they need the story to do.

directionInline.text: Kael's discomfort should be specific: not fear of being recognized, but dislike of becoming a usable symbol detached from his actual choices.

title: Do Not Bless It
summary: A group of locals asks Kael to publicly endorse their new committee under the Varnok name. Kael refuses to bless a political arrangement as a folk hero, but he agrees to sit and hear what they are actually trying to build.

panelPlan.text: Several locals bring a handwritten statement to Kael, asking Varnok to sign it so Marcus cannot come back claiming authority.
Eva sees the obvious usefulness. Jessa does not answer for Kael this time.
Kael reads the paper, then asks each person why they need a dead or absent man to make their own agreement legitimate.

dialogueInline.speaker: Local
dialogueInline.text: Marcus comes back, we show him Varnok backs us.

dialogueInline.speaker: Kael
dialogueInline.text: And if somebody else paints a Varnok who says he doesn't?

dialogueInline.speaker: Kael
dialogueInline.text: Maybe. But he'll know who he's dealing with.

directionInline.text: Do not let Kael become a constitutional fixer. His contribution is refusing borrowed legitimacy and forcing living people to own their choices.

title: Kael Mack
summary: Tomas thanks Kael under his real name in front of the room. The gesture is small but changes the trio: Eva has now seen a community member know exactly who Kael is, while Veyra has watched her false identity outlive her control.

panelPlan.text: At the door, Tomas calls Kael back and thanks him for cutting the rope. The room hears the name Kael Mack without erupting or correcting him.
Some patrons still raise cups to Varnok. Others shrug. Two names coexist because people are capable of knowing the truth and preferring the story.
On the road, Eva asks Jessa whether that counts as solving anything. Jessa says it solves one thing: Kael told the truth the first time.

dialogueInline.speaker: Veyra
dialogueInline.text: They know your name and kept Varnok.

dialogueInline.speaker: Tomas
dialogueInline.text: Some of us don't need him anymore.

directionInline.text: The issue should weaken the assumption that correcting the identity will correct the social effect. The town can know Kael and still keep Varnok.
